cards.headline: The Pomodoro Technique
lines: A popular method suggests 25 focused minutes of work, then a 5-minute break.
After four rounds, take a longer break.
Francesco Cirillo devised it in the late 1980s, named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.

cards.headline: Urgent isn't the same as important
lines: Sort tasks with two questions: is it urgent? Is it important?
Important-but-not-urgent work — planning, learning, health — is the easiest to neglect.
A popular method suggests it's often the work that matters most, so it deserves a slot in the day.
cards.source: Covey, 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' (1989), the Time Management Matrix.

cards.headline: If–then plans
lines: 'When it's 6 pm, I'll practise for 10 minutes' beats 'I'll practise more.'
Psychologist Peter Gollwitzer called these implementation intentions.
A review of 94 studies found they reliably improve follow-through.
cards.source: Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology.

cards.headline: Multitasking is really task-switching
lines: For demanding tasks, the brain mostly switches between them rather than doing both at once.
Every switch costs time and raises errors.
Batch similar tasks, and silence notifications while you focus.
cards.source: Rubinstein, Meyer & Evans (2001), J Exp Psychol: Human Perception and Performance; Monsell (2003), Trends Cogn Sci.

cards.headline: The two-minute rule
lines: A popular method suggests: if a task takes less than two minutes, do it now.
Its author, David Allen, argues that noting it down to come back to later costs more than just doing it.

cards.question: A standard Pomodoro is…
cards.why: 25 minutes of focus, then a short break. The method's author says the timer makes starting easier.

cards.question: Why does switching between demanding tasks slow you down?
options: The mind reloads each task's rules at every switch
cards.why: Experiments measure a 'switch cost' in time and errors as the mind reconfigures for each task.
cards.source: Monsell (2003), 'Task Switching', Trends in Cognitive Sciences.

cards.question: 'Work expands to fill the time available for its completion' is known as…
cards.why: C. Northcote Parkinson wrote it in The Economist in 1955. Shorter, set deadlines can counter it.

cards.question: Which of these is an implementation intention?
options: After dinner, I'll walk for 15 minutes
cards.why: It names a specific cue (after dinner) and a specific action, which makes follow-through more automatic.

cards.question: In Covey's urgent/important matrix, which kind of task does he say is easiest to neglect but often most valuable?
cards.why: A popular method suggests that planning, learning and health rarely shout for attention, so they get crowded out unless scheduled.
cards.source: Covey, 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' (1989).

cards.headline: The 80/20 rule is named after an economist
cards.text: Vilfredo Pareto showed in the 1890s that income and wealth were very unevenly spread; Joseph Juran later named the '80/20' principle after him. Real splits are rarely exactly 80/20.
cards.source: Pareto, 'Cours d'économie politique' (1896–97), on the distribution of income; Juran, 'Quality Control Handbook' (1951), who named the principle.

cards.headline: A plan quiets an unfinished task
cards.text: In experiments, making a specific plan for an unfinished goal reduced intrusive thoughts about it — even before the goal was done.
cards.source: Masicampo & Baumeister (2011), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.

cards.headline: Tiny interruptions cost more than they take
cards.text: In one study, interruptions of about three seconds were enough to roughly double error rates on a step-by-step task.
cards.source: Altmann, Trafton & Hambrick (2014), Journal of Experimental Psychology: General.

cards.headline: Brief breaks can protect focus
cards.text: In a vigilance experiment, people given two brief diversions kept their performance up, while those who worked straight through declined.
cards.source: Ariga & Lleras (2011), 'Brief and Rare Mental Breaks Keep You Focused', Cognition.

cards.headline: Building a habit that sticks

steps.headline: 1 · Make it obvious
lines: A popular method, James Clear's 'Atomic Habits', suggests putting the cue in sight: shoes by the door, a book on the pillow.
Habits start with a reliable trigger.

steps.headline: 2 · Make it small
lines: Start so small you can't say no: one push-up, one page.
Showing up matters more than size at first.

steps.headline: 3 · Stack it
lines: Attach the new habit to an old one: 'After I brush my teeth, I'll stretch.'
The old habit becomes the cue.

steps.headline: 4 · Give it time
lines: In one study, a new habit took a median of 66 days to become automatic, with wide variation.
Missing a single day didn't derail it.

cards.source: Step names after Clear, 'Atomic Habits' (2018); Lally et al. (2010), European Journal of Social Psychology; Fogg, 'Tiny Habits' (2019).

cards.headline: Productivity: the takeaways
points: Under two minutes? A popular rule says do it now.
